Abstract A female patient, aged 61 
years, who developed a severe im- 
mobilizing stiff-person syndrome in 
conjunction with insulin-dependent 
diabetes mellitus, is described. In ad- 
dition to the typical clinical symp- 
toms, diagnosis was proven by the 
presence of autoantibodies against 
glutamic acid decarboxylase in 
serum and cerebrospinal fluid. 
Symptomatic treatment with continu- 
ous intrathecal application of ba- 
clofen administered by a subcuta- 
neous pump resulted in rapid clinical 
improvement so that the patient be- 
came ambulatory. Intermittent with- 
drawal from intrathecal baclofen 
therapy led to complete remanifesta- 
tion of stiff-person syndrome within 
18 h; after re-introduction of in- 
trathecal therapy stiffness disap- 
peared completely within 48 h. The 
clinical course has been stable now 
for over 24 months and stiffness has 
completely disappeared. The effect 
of baclofen in this patient is dis- 
cussed in the light of the suggested 
pathophysiological mechanisms in 
stiff-person syndromes.

Case report 
One and a half years earlier, this 61-year-old woman had devel- 
oped chronically progressive painful stiffness of the musculature 
of her body, sparing arms and facial musculature. This stiffness 
initially included only the legs, but spread subsequently to the ab- 
domen, back and neck. Eventually, the patient could not walk or 
even sit. In addition, she complained of startle reactions with sud- 
denly increasing muscle stiffness caused by unexpected acoustic, 
visual or tactile stimuli. 
At the age of 40 years, the patient had developed type 1 dia- 
betes mellitus with greatly fluctuating blood sugar levels. Over the 
years, a diabetic retinopathy and a chronic compensated renal fail- 
ure had supervened. Autoimmune diseases were not known in the 
family. A biopsy of the gastrocnemius muscle performed else- 
where and an ascending lumbar myelography had revealed no ab- 
normality. Finally, the patient was admitted to our hospital. 
The bedridden patient was in a moderate general and nutri- 
tional condition. Her cranial nerves were normal. She was not able 
to bend her neck forwards. She could not move her legs at the hip, 
knee or ankle joints because of extreme muscle stiffness. The ab- 
dominal wall was hard as if with peritonitis. Hyperlordosis - often 
a feature of SPS - was not observed. There were no pareses or at- 
rophies. The tendon reflexes were normal in the upper and lower 
extremities, but induced severely painful muscle spasms of axial 
and leg muscles when elicited in the lower extremities. Plantar re- 
flexes were flexor. On sensory examination we found a distally 
pronounced mild diabetic polyneuropathy of the lower extremities 
involving all modalities except position sense. Coordination of her 
arms was normal, as were the findings of neuropsychological and 
psychopathological examinations. 
EMG showed continuous muscle activity similar to voluntary 
action. Electroneurography demonstrated a mild polyneuropathy 
of both sensory and motor nerves of the lower extremities, com- 
patible with the existing type 1 diabetes mellitus. Magnetic evoked 
motor potentials to the first interosseus and the tibialis anterior 
muscles were normal in amplitude and latency. Cranial MRI dis- 
closed some small white matter lesions of vascular origin on both 
sides. Except for an elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 
50/90 mm in the first two hours, blood sugar levels up to 800 mg/dl 
and reduced creatinine clearance (37 ml/min) with a corresponding 
elevation of creatinine to 1.5 mg/dl, routine laboratory findings were 
normal, including electrophoresis, C-reactive protein, rheumatoid 
factor, antinuclear antibodies, thyroid autoantibodies, thyroid hor- 
mones and treponemal agglutination test. Except for slightly posi- 
tive oligoclonal bands the cerebrospinal fluid was normal (cell 
count 3/mm 3, protein level 0.36 g/l, Delpeche ratio 0.49). GAD an- 
tibodies, as detmwnined immunocytochemically according to Soli- 
mena and coworkers [29], were strongly positive in CSF and 
serum. 
Having made the diagnosis of SPS by clinical and electrophys- 
iological criteria [5, 18, 22, 24] and demonstration of anti-GAD 
autoantihodies [12], we injected 2 mg diazepam intravenously, 
whereupon muscle tone and backache promptly diminished. The

patient could move her legs and bend her neck again (Fig. 1 ). None 
of the following intravenously administered drugs reduced the 
muscle tone or the painful spasms: insulin, isosorbide dinitrate, 
nifedipine, omeprazole, heparin, pethidine, buprenorphine, meta- 
mizole, diclofenac. Clonazepam and baclofen were then given 
orally at dosages of 1.5 mg and 20 mg daily, respectively, leading 
to improved mobility and relief of painful spasms. Higher doses 
were not tolerated and resulted in drowsiness. However, the patient 
was still unable to walk. Thereafter, bolus injections of up to 100 
btg baclofen were given intrathecally on consecutive days. Follow- 
ing injection of 75 gg, muscle tone decreased and backache im- 
proved further. After an even more successful injection of 1000 btg 
the patient received a subcutaneous port system in the epigastric 
region for continuous intrathecal application of baclofen. Baclofen 
was infused to titrate the required dosage further. With this treat- 
ment the patient started to walk, using crutches. After 2 weeks the 
port was removed and a pump subcutaneously implanted (Infusaid, 
Norwood, USA). With this pump a daily dosage of 260 btg ba- 
clofen was administered. A slightly higher dosage of 300 btg daily

Fig. 2 Polyelectromyographic recordings before (A), during with- 
drawal from intrathecal baclofen therapy (B) and 48 h after recon- 
tinuation (C). Calibrations are in mV and ms, respectively. Note 
the marked increase of muscle activity 18 h after onset of with- 
drawal from intrathecal baclofen therapy (B) 
resulted in drowsiness and nausea. Oral administration of clon- 
azepam and baclofen was discontinued. After 4 weeks of con- 
comitant physical therapy the patient's condition improved pro- 
gressively and she was finally able to walk with crutches (Fig. 1). 
Furthermore, effective immunosuppressive therapy with azathioprine 
(lymphocytes < 1000/gl) was initiated about 10 weeks after the 
start of the baclofen treatment. After a 12-month course of contin- 
uous treatment the patient had improved further: the gait pattern 
had normalized and only one crutch was needed (Fig. 1). At that 
time GAD autoantibodies were still detected in serum but were 
only weakly present in CSF. After 24 months her condition had 
stabilized further: gait was now normal, without crutches. At that 
time immunosuppression had to be discontinued because of severe 
lymphopenia. 
To prove that the intrathecal treatment with baclofen was still 
effective the patient was hospitalized and the baclofen therapy in- 
terrupted. Within 18 h the signs of SPS reappered to such a degree 
that the patient was no longer able to walk. Surface EMG record- 
ings from trunk and leg muscles again showed the typical sponta- 
neous muscle activity. After restoring the intrathecal baclofen ther- 
apy with the above-mentioned dosage of 260 gg the patient recov- 
ered completely within 48 h (Fig. 2).
